claim: YAP undergoes recurrent amplification in human SCC.
source: The transcriptional co-activator YAP undergoes recurrent amplification in human SCC and overexpression of YAP drives SCC formation in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hiemer et al., 2015; India Project Team of the International Cancer Genome Consortium, 2013) as stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Overexpression of YAP drives SCC formation in mice.
source: The transcriptional co-activator YAP undergoes recurrent amplification in human SCC and overexpression of YAP drives SCC formation in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011) as stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Human spSCC tumours feature strong nuclear localisation of YAP.
source: Here, we show that human spSCC tumours also feature strong nuclear localisation of YAP and overexpression of activated YAP (NLS-YAP-5SA) with Keratin-5 (K5-CreERt) is sufficient to induce rapid formation of both SCC and spSCC in mice.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of activated YAP (NLS-YAP-5SA) with Keratin-5 (K5-CreERt) is sufficient to induce rapid formation of both SCC and spSCC in mice.
source: Here, we show that human spSCC tumours also feature strong nuclear localisation of YAP and overexpression of activated YAP (NLS-YAP-5SA) with Keratin-5 (K5-CreERt) is sufficient to induce rapid formation of both SCC and spSCC in mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transgenic mouse model shown in Figure 2B and described in Results section.

claim: spSCC tumours arise at sites of epithelial scratch wounding.
source: spSCC tumours arise at sites of epithelial scratch wounding, where tumour-initiating epithelial cells undergo EMT to generate spSCC.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in transgenic mice shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tumour-initiating epithelial cells undergo EMT to generate spSCC.
source: spSCC tumours arise at sites of epithelial scratch wounding, where tumour-initiating epithelial cells undergo EMT to generate spSCC.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data (Figure 2C) and EMT marker expression (Figure 3).

claim: Expression of the EMT transcription factor ZEB1 arises upon wounding.
source: Expression of the EMT transcription factor ZEB1 arises upon wounding and is a defining characteristic of spSCC in mice and humans.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 3C-D and Figure 4A.

claim: ZEB1 is a defining characteristic of spSCC in mice and humans.
source: Expression of the EMT transcription factor ZEB1 arises upon wounding and is a defining characteristic of spSCC in mice and humans.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in mouse (Figure 3C) and human (Figure 5B) spSCC samples.

claim: The wound healing response synergises with YAP to drive metaplastic transformation of SCC to spSCC.
source: Thus, the wound healing response synergises with YAP to drive metaplastic transformation of SCC to spSCC.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that spSCC arises at wound sites and requires YAP overexpression.

claim: YAP is normally expressed primarily in the epidermis.
source: YAP is normally expressed primarily in the epidermis, and is nuclear localised in the basal layer stem progenitor cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: YAP is nuclear localised in the basal layer stem progenitor cells.
source: YAP is normally expressed primarily in the epidermis, and is nuclear localised in the basal layer stem progenitor cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: In spSCC tumours, YAP is strongly expressed and nuclear localised throughout the tumour.
source: In spSCC tumours, YAP is strongly expressed and nuclear localised throughout the tumour, despite the fact that the tumour is dermal rather than epidermal in character as revealed by the absence of K5 expression in the tumour (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: spSCC tumours are dermal rather than epidermal in character as revealed by the absence of K5 expression in the tumour.
source: In spSCC tumours, YAP is strongly expressed and nuclear localised throughout the tumour, despite the fact that the tumour is dermal rather than epidermal in character as revealed by the absence of K5 expression in the tumour (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: spSCC tumours are often associated with a wounded epidermis, as indicated by a gap in the K5-positive layer above the tumour.
source: We note that spSCC tumours are often associated with a wounded epidermis, as indicated by a gap in the K5-positive layer above the tumour.
evidence: Supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2B.

claim: NLS-YAP-5SA is able to induce formation of both SCC and spSCC in skin within 2–4 weeks of tamoxifen treatment.
source: We find that NLS-YAP-5SA is able to induce formation of both SCC and spSCC in skin within 2–4 weeks of tamoxifen treatment (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transgenic mouse model shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SCC and spSCC can be distinguished because spSCC tumour cells are dermally located and lack expression of K5.
source: SCC and spSCC can be distinguished because spSCC tumour cells are dermally located and lack expression of K5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: spSCC tumours tended to arise in regions where the mice scratch their skin.
source: Notably, spSCC tumours tended to arise in regions where the mice scratch their skin, and spSCC tumours were often associated with a wounded epidermis, while SCCs could arise in the absence of epidermal wounding (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: spSCC tumours were often associated with a wounded epidermis.
source: Notably, spSCC tumours tended to arise in regions where the mice scratch their skin, and spSCC tumours were often associated with a wounded epidermis, while SCCs could arise in the absence of epidermal wounding (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SCCs could arise in the absence of epidermal wounding.
source: Notably, spSCC tumours tended to arise in regions where the mice scratch their skin, and spSCC tumours were often associated with a wounded epidermis, while SCCs could arise in the absence of epidermal wounding (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both SCC and spSCC tumours arise from the K5-positive basal layer of the skin.
source: Lineage tracing with LacZ (encoding nuclear beta-Gal immunostained in brown) induced with the K5-CreERt line indicates that both SCC and spSCC tumours arise from the K5-positive basal layer of the skin (n = 22).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nuclear beta-Gal expression was detected in patches of epidermal cells in skin areas not subject to scratch wounds following treatment with tamoxifen for 5 days.
source: Following treatment with tamoxifen for 5 days, nuclear beta-Gal expression was detected in patches of epidermal cells in skin areas not subject to scratch wounds (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In regions subject to scratching, large spSCCs formed with clear nuclear beta-Gal expression in all tumour cells and some neighbouring epidermal cells.
source: In regions subject to scratching, large spSCCs formed with clear nuclear beta-Gal expression in all tumour cells and some neighbouring epidermal cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The spSCC tumours were highly proliferative, as indicated by Ki67-positive immunostaining.
source: The spSCC tumours were highly proliferative, as indicated by Ki67-positive immunostaining (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Oncogenic YAP drives spSCC formation by metaplastic transformation of K5-positive epidermal basal layer epithelial cells into K5-negative dermal mesenchymal spindle cells.
source: These results demonstrate that oncogenic YAP drives spSCC formation by metaplastic transformation of K5-positive epidermal basal layer epithelial cells into K5-negative dermal mesenchymal spindle cells.
evidence: Inferred from lineage tracing and marker expression data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Keratin-5 expression is inactivated upon transformation of SCC to spSCC following wounding in nuclear YAP-driven tumours.
source: In nuclear YAP-driven tumours, Keratin-5 expression is inactivated and Vimentin expression is strongly induced upon transformation of SCC to spSCC following wounding (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Vimentin expression is strongly induced upon transformation of SCC to spSCC following wounding in nuclear YAP-driven tumours.
source: In nuclear YAP-driven tumours, Keratin-5 expression is inactivated and Vimentin expression is strongly induced upon transformation of SCC to spSCC following wounding (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: ZEB1 mRNA and protein is normally not expressed in epithelial cells or SCC.
source: In vivo, we find that ZEB1 mRNA and protein is normally not expressed in epithelial cells or SCC but becomes strongly expressed in oncogenic YAP-driven spSCC tumour cells, similar to SNAIL1 mRNA (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: ZEB1 becomes strongly expressed in oncogenic YAP-driven spSCC tumour cells.
source: In vivo, we find that ZEB1 mRNA and protein is normally not expressed in epithelial cells or SCC but becomes strongly expressed in oncogenic YAP-driven spSCC tumour cells, similar to SNAIL1 mRNA (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: SNAIL1 mRNA becomes strongly expressed in oncogenic YAP-driven spSCC tumour cells.
source: In vivo, we find that ZEB1 mRNA and protein is normally not expressed in epithelial cells or SCC but becomes strongly expressed in oncogenic YAP-driven spSCC tumour cells, similar to SNAIL1 mRNA (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: YAP-driven spSCC arises via an EMT program involving expression of ZEB1.
source: These results indicate that YAP-driven spSCC arises via an EMT program involving expression of ZEB1.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of ZEB1 and other EMT markers in spSCC shown in Figure 3.

claim: ZEB1 is induced during the wound healing response in normal skin epithelia.
source: Importantly, we find that ZEB1 is also induced during the wound healing response in normal skin epithelia and in cultured skin keratinocytes (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: ZEB1 is induced during the wound healing response in cultured skin keratinocytes.
source: Importantly, we find that ZEB1 is also induced during the wound healing response in normal skin epithelia and in cultured skin keratinocytes (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of YAP activity with Dasatinib prevents activation of ZEB1 expression at 4 hr after scratch wounding.
source: We find that inhibition of YAP activity with this compound prevents activation of ZEB1 expression at 4 hr after scratch wounding (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Wound-induced ZEB1 expression is normally sustained by YAP activity.
source: These observations indicate that wound-induced ZEB1 expression is normally sustained by YAP activity.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that YAP/TAZ knockdown or Src inhibition prevents ZEB1 induction (Figure 4C,D).

claim: Silencing expression of TEAD1-4 with siRNAs prevented ZEB1 induction after scratch wounding.
source: To confirm that YAP acts via TEAD-dependent transcription, we silenced expression of TEAD1-4 with siRNAs, which prevented ZEB1 induction after scratch wounding (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: YAP acts via TEAD-dependent transcription to induce ZEB1.
source: To confirm that YAP acts via TEAD-dependent transcription, we silenced expression of TEAD1-4 with siRNAs, which prevented ZEB1 induction after scratch wounding (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inferred from TEAD knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TEAD1 binds to an upstream enhancer at the ZEB1 locus upon scratch wounding.
source: Finally, we were able to detect TEAD1 binding to an upstream enhancer at the ZEB1 locus upon scratch wounding, although the degree of enrichment is weak due to the very small percentage of ZEB1 expressing cells in this experiment (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by chromatin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The physiological upregulation of YAP and ZEB1 following wounding is only transient, as these genes are normally silenced following wound closure.
source: Importantly, the physiological upregulation of YAP and ZEB1 following wounding is only transient, as these genes are normally silenced following wound closure, which inhibits YAP.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of wound healing and YAP regulation.

claim: ZEB1 expression is not silenced in the presence of oncogenic NLS-YAP-5SA, allowing ZEB1 to drive EMT and spSCC formation.
source: In contrast, ZEB1 expression is not silenced in the presence of oncogenic NLS-YAP-5SA, allowing ZEB1 to drive EMT and spSCC formation (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Inferred from persistent ZEB1 expression in NLS-YAP-5SA driven spSCC shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ZEB1 becomes co-expressed with YAP in human spSCC tumours.
source: We first confirmed that ZEB1 becomes co-expressed with YAP and that there is a loss of E-cadherin and gain of Vimentin expression in human spSCC tumours (Figure 5A–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data on human samples shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: There is a loss of E-cadherin in human spSCC tumours.
source: We first confirmed that ZEB1 becomes co-expressed with YAP and that there is a loss of E-cadherin and gain of Vimentin expression in human spSCC tumours (Figure 5A–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data on human samples shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is a gain of Vimentin expression in human spSCC tumours.
source: We first confirmed that ZEB1 becomes co-expressed with YAP and that there is a loss of E-cadherin and gain of Vimentin expression in human spSCC tumours (Figure 5A–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data on human samples shown in Figure 5C.

claim: YAP is a driver of both SCC and spSCC formation.
source: In conclusion, our findings identify YAP as a driver of both SCC and spSCC formation, demonstrate that both SCC and spSCC originate in the basal layer of the epidermis, and reveal that the SCC versus spSCC outcome is determined by whether or not tumour cells undergo a ZEB1-mediated EMT program that can be induced by skin wounding (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from transgenic mouse models shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both SCC and spSCC originate in the basal layer of the epidermis.
source: In conclusion, our findings identify YAP as a driver of both SCC and spSCC formation, demonstrate that both SCC and spSCC originate in the basal layer of the epidermis, and reveal that the SCC versus spSCC outcome is determined by whether or not tumour cells undergo a ZEB1-mediated EMT program that can be induced by skin wounding (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The SCC versus spSCC outcome is determined by whether or not tumour cells undergo a ZEB1-mediated EMT program that can be induced by skin wounding.
source: In conclusion, our findings identify YAP as a driver of both SCC and spSCC formation, demonstrate that both SCC and spSCC originate in the basal layer of the epidermis, and reveal that the SCC versus spSCC outcome is determined by whether or not tumour cells undergo a ZEB1-mediated EMT program that can be induced by skin wounding (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that spSCC requires both YAP and wounding, and expresses ZEB1.

claim: SCC reflects an abnormal hyperactivation of homeostatic epidermal proliferation mechanisms requiring YAP/TAZ but not ZEB1.
source: Thus, while SCC reflects an abnormal hyperactivation of homeostatic epidermal proliferation mechanisms (requiring YAP/TAZ (Debaugnies et al., 2018) but not ZEB1, which is not expressed in SCC), spSCC reflects an abnormal hyperactivation of wound repair proliferation and EMT mechanisms (driven by both YAP and ZEB1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SCC does not express ZEB1 (Figure 3C-D) and requires YAP/TAZ (cited from Debaugnies et al., 2018).

claim: spSCC reflects an abnormal hyperactivation of wound repair proliferation and EMT mechanisms driven by both YAP and ZEB1.
source: Thus, while SCC reflects an abnormal hyperactivation of homeostatic epidermal proliferation mechanisms (requiring YAP/TAZ (Debaugnies et al., 2018) but not ZEB1, which is not expressed in SCC), spSCC reflects an abnormal hyperactivation of wound repair proliferation and EMT mechanisms (driven by both YAP and ZEB1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that spSCC expresses both YAP and ZEB1 and arises at wound sites.

claim: Exposure of skin to trauma, burns or ionizing radiation are commonly associated with spSCC formation in patients.
source: Overall, our findings begin to provide a molecular understanding of how genetic changes lead to SCC tumour growth and subsequent transformation to spSCC, and explain why exposure of skin to trauma, burns or ionizing radiation are so commonly associated with spSCC formation in patients (McKee, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior clinical observations (McKee, 1996).

claim: YAP was originally discovered to drive cell proliferation in Drosophila.
source: Recent work has identified the YAP oncoprotein, originally discovered to drive cell proliferation in Drosophila (Huang et al., 2005), and later to drive liver tumours in mice (Camargo et al., 2007; Dong et al., 2007) and to be mechanically regulated (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Huang et al., 2005).

claim: YAP drives liver tumours in mice.
source: Recent work has identified the YAP oncoprotein, originally discovered to drive cell proliferation in Drosophila (Huang et al., 2005), and later to drive liver tumours in mice (Camargo et al., 2007; Dong et al., 2007) and to be mechanically regulated (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Camargo et al., 2007; Dong et al., 2007).

claim: YAP is mechanically regulated.
source: Recent work has identified the YAP oncoprotein, originally discovered to drive cell proliferation in Drosophila (Huang et al., 2005), and later to drive liver tumours in mice (Camargo et al., 2007; Dong et al., 2007) and to be mechanically regulated (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Dupont et al., 2011).

claim: YAP is a driver of epidermal cell proliferation in mouse embryos.
source: In skin, YAP is a driver of epidermal cell proliferation in mouse embryos (Zhang et al., 2011) and SCC formation in embryonic mouse skin after transplantation into nude mice (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2011).

claim: YAP drives SCC formation in embryonic mouse skin after transplantation into nude mice.
source: In skin, YAP is a driver of epidermal cell proliferation in mouse embryos (Zhang et al., 2011) and SCC formation in embryonic mouse skin after transplantation into nude mice (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Schlegelmilch et al., 2011).

claim: YAP knockouts prevent Ras-driven skin SCC formation.
source: YAP knockouts also prevent Ras-driven skin SCC formation (Debaugnies et al., 2018; Zanconato et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Debaugnies et al., 2018; Zanconato et al., 2015).

claim: YAP promotes human SCC cell proliferation in culture.
source: YAP is furthermore known to exhibit recurrent amplifications in human SCC tumours (Hiemer et al., 2015; India Project Team of the International Cancer Genome Consortium, 2013) and to promote human SCC cell proliferation in culture (Walko et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Walko et al., 2017).

claim: YAP acts redundantly with its paralog TAZ to maintain proliferation of basal layer stem/progenitor cells during normal skin development and homeostasis.
source: During normal skin development and homeostasis, YAP acts redundantly with its paralog TAZ to maintain proliferation of basal layer stem/progenitor cells and to promote wound healing (Elbediwy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Elbediwy et al., 2016).

claim: YAP acts redundantly with TAZ to promote wound healing.
source: During normal skin development and homeostasis, YAP acts redundantly with its paralog TAZ to maintain proliferation of basal layer stem/progenitor cells and to promote wound healing (Elbediwy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Elbediwy et al., 2016).

claim: Integrin-SRC signalling promotes YAP activity in cell culture, mouse skin and in human SCC cells in culture.
source: Integrin-SRC signalling promotes YAP activity in cell culture, mouse skin and in human SCC cells in culture (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Kim and Gumbiner, 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Kim and Gumbiner, 2015; Li et al., 2016).

claim: The cell type of origin for spSCC is thought to be epithelial, but is still not definitively established.
source: The cell type of origin for spSCC is thought to be epithelial, but is still not definitively established.
evidence: Based on existing scientific literature and uncertainty in the field.

claim: Histological analysis of spindle cell carcinomas identified a 'sarcomatoid' morphology, resembling the mesenchymal fibroblasts of malignant fibrosarcomas.
source: Histological analysis of spindle cell carcinomas identified a 'sarcomatoid' morphology, resembling the mesenchymal fibroblasts of malignant fibrosarcomas, which suggests a possible mesodermal origin.
evidence: Based on established histological observations in the field.

claim: The spindle-shaped tumour cells of spSCC may derive from epithelial cells of the epidermis via an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: However, the spindle-shaped tumour cells of spSCC may instead derive from epithelial cells of the epidermis via an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Brabletz et al., 2018; Yang and Weinberg, 2008), a process observed to occur in some mouse models of RasG12D-driven skin carcinomas (Latil et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on EMT (Brabletz et al., 2018; Yang and Weinberg, 2008; Latil et al., 2017).

claim: EMT is a process observed to occur in some mouse models of RasG12D-driven skin carcinomas.
source: However, the spindle-shaped tumour cells of spSCC may instead derive from epithelial cells of the epidermis via an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Brabletz et al., 2018; Yang and Weinberg, 2008), a process observed to occur in some mouse models of RasG12D-driven skin carcinomas (Latil et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Latil et al., 2017).

claim: A defining feature of EMT is the downregulation of epithelial markers such E-cadherin or Keratins and upregulation of Vimentin.
source: A defining feature of EMT is the downregulation of epithelial markers such E-cadherin or Keratins and upregulation of Vimentin.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of EMT processes.

claim: EMT is known to be driven by E-box DNA binding transcription factors such as Twist (mammalian TWIST1), Snail (mammalian SNAI1 and SNAI2/SLUG), and Zfh1/2 (mammalian ZEB1/2).
source: EMT is known to be driven by E-box DNA binding transcription factors such as Twist (mammalian TWIST1), Snail (mammalian SNAI1 and SNAI2/SLUG), and Zfh1/2 (mammalian ZEB1/2) – all originally discovered in Drosophila, and then in other model organisms, to promote mesodermal rather than ectodermal fate during developmental EMT (Boulay et al., 1987; Broihier et al., 1998; Fortini et al., 1991; Lai et al., 1991, 1993; Leptin, 1991; Nieto et al., 1992, 1994; Thisse et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on EMT transcription factors.

claim: In Drosophila, Zfh1/2 are expressed downstream of Twist and Snail.
source: We chose to focus on ZEB1 because (1) in Drosophila, Zfh1/2 are expressed downstream of Twist and Snail (Lai et al., 1991), (2) in mammalian cells in culture, ZEB1 (also called deltaEF1) and ZEB2 (also called SIP1) are known to be potent inducers of EMT (Aigner et al., 2007; Comijn et al., 2001; Eger et al., 2005; Krebs et al., 2017) and (3) ZEB1 was recently shown to cooperate with YAP to drive a common set of target genes in cell culture (Lehmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lai et al., 1991).

claim: In mammalian cells in culture, ZEB1 (also called deltaEF1) and ZEB2 (also called SIP1) are known to be potent inducers of EMT.
source: We chose to focus on ZEB1 because (1) in Drosophila, Zfh1/2 are expressed downstream of Twist and Snail (Lai et al., 1991), (2) in mammalian cells in culture, ZEB1 (also called deltaEF1) and ZEB2 (also called SIP1) are known to be potent inducers of EMT (Aigner et al., 2007; Comijn et al., 2001; Eger et al., 2005; Krebs et al., 2017) and (3) ZEB1 was recently shown to cooperate with YAP to drive a common set of target genes in cell culture (Lehmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Aigner et al., 2007; Comijn et al., 2001; Eger et al., 2005; Krebs et al., 2017).

claim: ZEB1 was recently shown to cooperate with YAP to drive a common set of target genes in cell culture.
source: We chose to focus on ZEB1 because (1) in Drosophila, Zfh1/2 are expressed downstream of Twist and Snail (Lai et al., 1991), (2) in mammalian cells in culture, ZEB1 (also called deltaEF1) and ZEB2 (also called SIP1) are known to be potent inducers of EMT (Aigner et al., 2007; Comijn et al., 2001; Eger et al., 2005; Krebs et al., 2017) and (3) ZEB1 was recently shown to cooperate with YAP to drive a common set of target genes in cell culture (Lehmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Lehmann et al., 2016).

claim: Dasatinib is a Src family kinase inhibitor that is known to strongly inhibit YAP activation.
source: To inhibit YAP activation, we treated scratch-wounded keratinocyte monolayers with either siRNAs targeting YAP/TAZ or with the Src family kinase inhibitor Dasatinib, which is known to strongly inhibit YAP activation (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Kim and Gumbiner, 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Kim and Gumbiner, 2015; Li et al., 2016).

claim: Transfection with siRNAs against YAP/TAZ prevents induction of ZEB1 at the leading edge after scratch wounding.
source: Induction of ZEB1 at the leading edge is prevented by transfection with siRNAs against YAP/TAZ. Scale bar 50 μM.
evidence: Supported by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment with Dasatinib prevents induction of ZEB1 at the leading edge after scratch wounding.
source: Induction of ZEB1 at the leading edge is prevented by treatment with Dasatinib, a Src-family kinase inhibitor that prevents YAP activation. Scale bar 50 μM.
evidence: Supported by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment with siRNAs against TEAD1-4 prevents induction of ZEB1 at the leading edge after scratch wounding.
source: Induction of ZEB1 at the leading edge is prevented by treatment with siRNAs against TEAD1-4. Scale bar 50 μM.
evidence: Supported by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Punch wounding of mouse skin induces ZEB1 immunostaining in some leading edge cells.
source: Punch wounding of mouse skin induces ZEB1 immunostaining in some leading edge cells. Scale bars 100 μM.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Scratch wounding of skin keratinocytes in culture induces ZEB1 and YAP immunostaining in leading edge cells.
source: Scratch wounding of skin keratinocytes in culture induces ZEB1 and YAP immunostaining in leading edge cells. Scale bar 50 μM.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.
